abstract: Cardenolides are naturally occurring steroidal derivatives that function as chemical defense compounds. These natural products are also widely used in medicine, as exemplified by the use of digitoxin in treating cardiac disease. Although cardenolides are most widely known as plant-derived natural products, these compounds are also produced in certain beetle species. However, while the biosynthesis of cardenolides has been well-studied in plants, it is not known how insects produce these compounds. Here we report the identification of a cardenolide biosynthetic enzyme from the leaf beetle Chrysolina coerulans. This cytochrome P450, CcCYP9Z273, catalyzes an array of steroid oxidations, including the conversion of pregnenolone into caraumbellogenin through C14-hydroxylation. Gene silencing suggests that CcCYP9Z273 is essential for beetle cardenolide formation and isotope tracing experiments support caraumbellogenin as an on-pathway biosynthetic intermediate. Mutagenesis of CcCYP9Z273 identifies an active-site residue that controls the enzyme product selectivity between C14- and C15-hydroxylation. These findings establish an early step in beetle cardenolide biosynthesis and highlight how distinct enzyme families have been recruited in insects and plants to generate a shared intermediate in the biosynthesis of these important metabolites.
